title: Ashtpadi 1, salok: I bow to the Guru
hook: aad gure namah: I bow to the primal Guru, the Guru of the ages, the True Guru (Sukhmani 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, how people read Sukhmani, and your line: one ashtpadi at a time. Did your slot make it into the calendar? Today we open the first one, starting with its salok. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

Before a match, a wrestler in a Punjabi village touches the earth of the pit and then his forehead. A musician touches the strings of an instrument before playing, a dancer bows to the floor. Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib when they come into its presence. Each one begins a serious thing by lowering the head a little, first. The long road of Sukhmani begins like that too. Before a single teaching, before peace or Name or anything else, Guru Arjan bows. Four times.
screen: `A WRESTLER TOUCHES THE EARTH.` → `SERIOUS THINGS BEGIN WITH A BOW.` → `SUKHMANI OPENS: FOUR BOWS.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok that opens Sukhmani. Aad gure namah. Jugaad gure namah. Satgure namah. Sri gurdeve namah. Each line ends with namah, a word of homage: I bow, I salute. So the salok is four bows, each to a slightly different face of the same Guru. Aad gure: the Guru of the beginning, the primal Guru, there before anything began. Jugaad gure: the Guru through all the ages, jug being the great ages of time. Satgure: the True Guru. And Sri gurdeve: the great, divine Guru, the Guru who shines. Who is this Guru? In the Sikh reading of this salok, the Guru is God, the One who teaches. Sikhs also honor the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru's voice in the world, but here the bows go to the One beyond time: the beginning, every age, truth itself. Listen to how the salok moves. It starts at the very beginning, then stretches across all ages, then names what is true, then what shines. A bow that travels from the first moment to this one. Some listeners hear an echo of Japji's opening salok, which praises the One who was true in the beginning and true through the ages. Guru Arjan is setting Sukhmani in the same frame. And notice the order he chooses: the jewel of peace doesn't begin with peace. It begins with bowing. Peace, the bani suggests, starts with the head a little lower than before.
screen: `NAMAH: I BOW.` · `THE PRIMAL GURU, THE GURU OF AGES.` · `THE TRUE GURU, THE DIVINE GURU.` · `PEACE BEGINS WITH A BOW.` · then, large: `I BOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow your head once. Sit up comfortably. Breathe in. As you breathe out, let your head lower slowly, chin toward your chest, as far as feels easy. Stay there for a breath or two, and notice what it feels like to be lower than a moment ago. Then rise slowly. If you'd like, repeat it four times, one bow for each line: the beginning, the ages, the true, the divine. If you pray, you can whisper aad gure namah. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 1. The first section of Sukhmani, opened by a salok of four bows: to the primal Guru, the Guru of the ages, the True Guru, the divine Guru.
Your line: I bow. Today, before one serious thing, a meeting, a meal, a hard conversation, lower your head a little for one breath first. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: I bow is just a polite opening.
what it means: four bows to the One as Guru, at the beginning, through the ages, as truth, as the divine.
what a scholar hears: the salok uses Sanskritic forms (gure, namah, gurdeve), and its frame of aad and jugaad recalls the opening salok of Japji.

notes: Salok transliterated 'aad gure namah, jugaad gure namah, satgure namah, sri gurdeve namah' and glossed; confirm.
Reading 'the Guru' here as God the teacher, with the Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib honored as the Guru's voice: confirm wording.
Wrestler touching the pit's earth: a common akhara custom, phrased generally; confirm or soften.
Echo of Japji's opening salok (aad sach, jugaad sach) offered as 'some listeners hear'; confirm.
